Speaker: A:
Text: We are here with Mrs. Barbara Sharpe at the Kirby Smith building in Gainesville.

Speaker: A:
Text: It’s November 8th.

Speaker: A:
Text: And I would like to start off by thanking you, Ms. Sharpe, for agreeing to do the interview with me.

Speaker: S:
Text: You are quite welcome.

Speaker: A:
Text: Could you start by telling me when and where you were born and what it was like to grow up in that area?

Speaker: S:
Text: Okay, I was born in Quincy, Florida.

Speaker: S:
Text: However, I don’t remember living there because my parents left there, actually, when I was a baby.

Speaker: S:
Text: And we moved to Seminole County in Sanford.

Speaker: S:
Text: Now, I remember living in Sanford.

Speaker: S:
Text: And I liked Sanford, it was a celery city.

Speaker: S:
Text: My father was in the Navy.

Speaker: S:
Text: And my mother just took care of us.

Speaker: S:
Text: And so, you know, I just enjoyed my growing up there.

Speaker: S:
Text: We had a guava tree in our backyard.

Speaker: S:
Text: And so it was just fun.

Speaker: S:
Text: I was just a typical child.

Speaker: S:
Text: And we lived in a nice area.

Speaker: A:
Text: Okay.

Speaker: S:
Text: Uh-huh.

Speaker: A:
Text: Was the area you lived in predominately White or African American or mixed?

Speaker: S:
Text: It was mixed.

Speaker: A:
Text: It was mixed?

Speaker: S:
Text: Mmhm.

Speaker: S:
Text: The area that I lived in, it was not apartments like the Section 8 apartments or anything like that — no.

Speaker: S:
Text: We were in a home.

Speaker: A:
Text: You were in a home?

Speaker: S:
Text: Uh-huh.

Speaker: S:
Text: And so I enjoyed that.

Speaker: S:
Text: I also remember my mother during the time was saying that they had to get stamps for sugar and stuff like that.

Speaker: S:
Text: That was a long time ago.

Speaker: S:
Text: And I went to school there.

Speaker: S:
Text: I could walk to school and I went to school there in elementary school.

Speaker: S:
Text: Moved there, from there to Gainesville.

Speaker: S:
Text: To Alachua County.

Speaker: S:
Text: And I moved from Alachua County to Putnam County, back to Alachua.

Speaker: S:
Text: I spent most of my life here in Alachua County.

Speaker: A:
Text: Did you move around because of your father’s job?

Speaker: S:
Text: That’s where my father was.

Speaker: S:
Text: My father was from there, my mother actually was from Quincy.

Speaker: A:
Text: Oh okay.

Speaker: S:
Text: Mmhm.

Speaker: A:
Text: As a teenager did you work anywhere?

Speaker: S:
Text: Yes, I did.

Speaker: S:
Text: I tell you what: when I was in school — the superintendent had a — my mother had a certificate, which I don’t even think they give those things anymore.

Speaker: S:
Text: I had a certificate so that I could go to school three days out of the week and work two, and to help my mom.

Speaker: S:
Text: And so I did that, but there was a stipulation that I had to be able to keep my grades up in order to do that.

Speaker: S:
Text: And I did it, and so it turned out fine.

Speaker: S:
Text: I worked at a doctor’s office.

Speaker: A:
Text: Oh, really?

Speaker: A:
Text: Did you enjoy that?

Speaker: S:
Text: Yes, I really did, I loved that.

Speaker: S:
Text: He kinda, like, yeah, was kinda second father or something.

Speaker: A:
Text: Oh, that’s nice.

Speaker: A:
Text: When you went to school those three days a week, can you describe the experience?

Speaker: A:
Text: Was there segregation still going on?

Speaker: S:
Text: Yes.

Speaker: A:
Text: Did you face it?

Speaker: S:
Text: Yes, there was segregation during all that time.

Speaker: S:
Text: However, I did not know that it was segregation.

Speaker: S:
Text: And the reason I did not know it was because I was not used to mixing with other kids.

Speaker: S:
Text: You know, just my own race was what I used to.

Speaker: S:
Text: So, I didn’t know anything about it until later on.

Speaker: S:
Text: Early on I didn’t, because I thought that’s the way it's supposed to be.

Speaker: S:
Text: I thought everybody was like that, you know.

Speaker: S:
Text: So I didn’t consider it a bad thing.

Speaker: S:
Text: It might not have been the best thing, but I didn’t think it was that bad either.

Speaker: S:
Text: You know, 'cause I was growing up and I thought that was the way it supposed to been.

Speaker: S:
Text: My mother kinda raised us that — this is one thing that I believe all of us carry to this day, is that when we were growing up and then we were learning, my mother told us that nobody was any better than we were.

Speaker: S:
Text: We were different, but nobody was any better.

Speaker: S:
Text: That we were just as important as anybody else and she wanted us always to remember that.

Speaker: S:
Text: And I always thought I was something and I still do.

Speaker: S:
Text: That helped me.

Speaker: S:
Text: That helped me.

Speaker: S:
Text: So, you know, I did pretty good behind that.

Speaker: A:
Text: When you look back, can you remember any instances where you didn’t realize that was segregation then, but now you’re like, “Oh, gosh”?

Speaker: S:
Text: Mmhm.

Speaker: S:
Text: Because we lived in Putnam County, we used to have to drive by White schools.

Speaker: S:
Text: And then, you know, that was when I was getting on up in the grades.

Speaker: S:
Text: And I thought, you know, now that I look back: how come, you know, we had to ride by schools when we couldn’t stop there, you know?

Speaker: S:
Text: But that’s when I knew, you know, that that was segregation.

Speaker: S:
Text: And it probably shouldn’t have been that way.

Speaker: S:
Text: But if I was affected by it, I did not know it.

Speaker: S:
Text: Cause my mother and father were very good parents.

Speaker: S:
Text: So, we had good food, I mean, we had good clothing, and all that kind of stuff.

Speaker: S:
Text: So, I was okay with that.

Speaker: A:
Text: Do you think the education you received at your school was equivalent or better than the one at the White schools?

Speaker: A:
Text: I think to me it was pretty good because I was able to learn and I was able to take the materials that we had and learn.

Speaker: A:
Text: And that helped me to get where I am today.

Speaker: A:
Text: Now, to say that it was equal to what the other kids had — the other race had — I don’t know.

Speaker: A:
Text: But I was told that we had hand-me-down books.

Speaker: A:
Text: That some of the books that we got were — the pages were torn out of them, they were old books after everybody else had done them.

Speaker: A:
Text: Then they were passed down to us.

Speaker: A:
Text: But I did the best I could with what I had, and so I'm comfortable with that.

Speaker: A:
Text: So you went to which high school?

Speaker: S:
Text: I went in Seminole County.

Speaker: S:
Text: It was Hopper Academy.

Speaker: S:
Text: That was an elementary school.

Speaker: A:
Text: And now you continued on to go to college?

Speaker: S:
Text: Oh yeah.

Speaker: S:
Text: But what I did was, when I got married and had my children, my top priority was to get my kids educated.

Speaker: S:
Text: Which they were not in segregation — everything was, you know, leveled off.

Speaker: S:
Text: And that was my first priority.

Speaker: S:
Text: Well, at one point in my life, I was in college right along with my kids.

Speaker: A:
Text: Oh!

Speaker: S:
Text: Mmhm.

Speaker: S:
Text: I started at Santa Fe and I graduated from Santa Fe.

Speaker: S:
Text: I was in the first honors class there.

Speaker: S:
Text: And then that rested for a while, because they were coming on up and I had to give them, you know, a lot of attention, which they deserved.

Speaker: S:
Text: It was their turn.

Speaker: S:
Text: So I did that but later I started at the University of Florida.

Speaker: S:
Text: However, I was such a nontraditional student until I could not get the classes that I needed.

Speaker: S:
Text: I was going to go into social work.

Speaker: S:
Text: And the transfer had already been done for me coming from Santa Fe and I was already accepted into the — what is it?

Speaker: A:
Text: University of Florida?

Speaker: S:
Text: Yeah, University of Florida social — gosh, what is it?

Speaker: S:
Text: I can’t even think of the name of it.

Speaker: S:
Text: But the dean over that department, he’d already approved it and everything.

Speaker: S:
Text: But I didn’t go then.

Speaker: S:
Text: So, I started going, just taking a few classes.

Speaker: S:
Text: But I could not make it.

Speaker: S:
Text: But I did good though!

Speaker: S:
Text: But I couldn’t make it because they weren’t offering the classes I needed at night.

Speaker: S:
Text: Because I would need to, you know.

Speaker: S:
Text: So, I went to Nova Southeastern.

Speaker: S:
Text: There was a satellite over here off of 13th Street.

Speaker: S:
Text: So I went there and I got a degree in — a Bachelor of Science degree.

Speaker: S:
Text: I got an Associate of Science at Santa Fe and then I got a Bachelor of Science at Nova Southeastern, in Business and Professional Management.

Speaker: S:
Text: Uh-huh.

Speaker: S:
Text: And then, later on, I became a school board member.

Speaker: S:
Text: I ran.

Speaker: S:
Text: I had no idea that I was going to win or lose.

Speaker: S:
Text: I just knew that the experience I had had with my children and that I had had with my self would qualify me to be a good school board member.

Speaker: S:
Text: So I ran in '92 and I won.

Speaker: S:
Text: The very first time.

Speaker: A:
Text: Congratulations!

Speaker: S:
Text: Thank you.

Speaker: S:
Text: The first female, Black female, to be elected since Reconstruction.

Speaker: S:
Text: I thought that was pretty good.

Speaker: A:
Text: Wow!

Speaker: A:
Text: That’s impressive.

Speaker: S:
Text: So then I did that.

Speaker: S:
Text: I did all of that.

Speaker: S:
Text: And that’s a lot of work also.

Speaker: S:
Text: And I was never a teacher or anything like that.

Speaker: S:
Text: But I believe that I was not at a disadvantage because I wasn’t a teacher, because everybody don’t need to be teacher -- having had to be on the school board.

Speaker: S:
Text: You need a variety.

Speaker: S:
Text: I came from business.

Speaker: A:
Text: Mmhm.

Speaker: S:
Text: And my husband and I owned a little community store, little grocery store we called “Pit Stop.”

Speaker: S:
Text: “Pit Stop Community Store.”

Speaker: S:
Text: And he was a barber.

Speaker: S:
Text: He was in with his grandfather, his uncle, and another male was in there.

Speaker: S:
Text: So he ran a barber shop.

Speaker: S:
Text: But then he — after the grandfather died and the uncle died — they kinda closed that down, he became a housing inspector for the city of Gainesville.

Speaker: S:
Text: So, he developed lung cancer and there was a lot of stress.

Speaker: S:
Text: So, we closed the grocery store down and he was fine.

Speaker: S:
Text: They went in, they found out that he had just a little tiny spot on his lung.

Speaker: S:
Text: And so, they were able to take care of that and everything and he did not have to receive blood, no radiation, no chemo or anything.

Speaker: S:
Text: And that was in 1982.

Speaker: S:
Text: And he’s awesome today.

Speaker: A:
Text: That’s wonderful.

Speaker: S:
Text: He gets his check-ups everyday.

Speaker: S:
Text: He’s a survivor.

Speaker: S:
Text: And so then -- but I'm still constantly doing my -- and then my daughters graduated from high school.

Speaker: S:
Text: They all have college degrees.

Speaker: S:
Text: I have two that graduated from Florida A&M University and one that graduated from Bethune-Cookman College.

Speaker: S:
Text: And they’re rivals, of course.

Speaker: S:
Text: Can’t talk about it 'round my house.

Speaker: S:
Text: And so I think that I did a lot of good on the school board 'cause I was elected in 1992, I got off of my own volition in 2004, and I was recruited to come back.

Speaker: S:
Text: So in 2008, I did.

Speaker: S:
Text: I ran again — never have been done before, the same person on two time.

Speaker: S:
Text: But I was recruited.

Speaker: S:
Text: And I thought, well, I’m not doing anything anyways, so I’ll try it to see what happens.

Speaker: S:
Text: So I did, and I won again, and here I am.

Speaker: A:
Text: Oh my gosh, that’s wonderful.

Speaker: S:
Text: Now during that time, I championed some things.

Speaker: S:
Text: I was appointed by governor Lawton Chiles to the Healthy Kids program.

Speaker: S:
Text: I don’t think it’s Healthy Kids anymore, it’s something else.

Speaker: S:
Text: I was appointed to the board of directors.

Speaker: S:
Text: So then, after that, I came here and started the Healthy Kids program here in Alachua County.

Speaker: S:
Text: Because our kids were using the emergency room as their primary source of care.

Speaker: S:
Text: So any kid that was not on Medicaid, they qualified for the Healthy Kids.

Speaker: S:
Text: The people who were very, very low socioeconomics had to pay nothing.

Speaker: S:
Text: The people who could pay something, they were on a sliding scale.

Speaker: S:
Text: But it was still not the amount — it had to do with their income.

Speaker: S:
Text: And so I did that.

Speaker: S:
Text: I was really proud of that.

Speaker: S:
Text: But when the state kinda changed the name — KidCare, I think they did.

Speaker: A:
Text: Yeah, I think I’ve heard of that.

Speaker: S:
Text: We had very, very few that maybe in Alachua — under Healthy Kids at the school system.

Speaker: S:
Text: But we do have the KidCare around Alachua County.

Speaker: S:
Text: So then I did chess.

Speaker: S:
Text: There was just a few.

Speaker: S:
Text: Mr. Pine, there was a man named George Pine, that had started just some chess in maybe one or two schools.

Speaker: S:
Text: So I championed chess.

Speaker: S:
Text: I did a lot of research on it from New York, from this man in New York.

Speaker: S:
Text: I forgot his name.

Speaker: S:
Text: Because it was a myth that Black kids, or low socioeconomic kids period, but particularly Black kids, they couldn't learn as well.

Speaker: S:
Text: So they couldn't play chess.

Speaker: S:
Text: Now that was the myth that was going on at that time, particularly in New York and Harlem.

Speaker: S:
Text: But it was going around, you know, everywhere and people just weren't interested in trying to see whether that was true or not.

Speaker: S:
Text: But this guy did in Harlem and found out that those kids excelled.

Speaker: S:
Text: Well, I initiated that and got us chess into most of our afterschool programs and most of our schools that were interested.

Speaker: S:
Text: And so, and now chess is still going on.

Speaker: S:
Text: Let me see what else did I champion now.

Speaker: S:
Text: There's a program in this district called the teacher — excuse me.

Speaker: S:
Text: It's an orientation program for new teachers.

Speaker: S:
Text: I championed that.

Speaker: S:
Text: It's still going on.

Speaker: S:
Text: It's very good.

Speaker: S:
Text: We have gotten great reviews and responses on it and it's a very good thing.

Speaker: S:
Text: People love it.

Speaker: S:
Text: It started out as being new teachers but I wanted it to be for veteran teachers too.

Speaker: S:
Text: But I felt like the new teachers needed it most.

Speaker: S:
Text: So, we kinda geared it toward that because, you know, they need it most.

Speaker: S:
Text: But it's a very good program.

Speaker: S:
Text: I'm proud of that.

Speaker: S:
Text: What else?

Speaker: S:
Text: Oh, uniforms.

Speaker: S:
Text: I championed uniforms.

Speaker: S:
Text: I tried to get 'em back in 1994.

Speaker: S:
Text: And I had — you gotta have 3, you gotta be able to count to 3.

Speaker: S:
Text: You gotta have 3 board members who think a lot.

Speaker: S:
Text: But I did, at the time, I thought.

Speaker: S:
Text: But then some of them went and got to the wire and they started getting criticisms.

Speaker: S:
Text: They changed their mind.

Speaker: S:
Text: Well, you know, I felt like it was worth just going to battle for because it wasn't helping me, it was helping the kids.

Speaker: S:
Text: Took all of the competiveness out of it.

Speaker: S:
Text: The peer-driven fashion shows where the girls showing too much skin, the boys are coming down with that.

Speaker: S:
Text: And it's just a shame.

Speaker: S:
Text: Takes the focus away from learning and all that kind of thing.

Speaker: S:
Text: So that helped a lot.

Speaker: S:
Text: The very first day of school — now, we started that last year.

Speaker: S:
Text: The very first day of school, we had — the superintendent and I, and some of our other staff, we travelled around to the schools, all the schools, and people were saying it’s the best first day of school that they had seen in years.

Speaker: S:
Text: And so that turned out good, and it happened again this year.

Speaker: A:
Text: So there are still uniforms?

Speaker: S:
Text: Uh-huh.

Speaker: S:
Text: We're still uniformed.

Speaker: S:
Text: We had made a policy of it.

Speaker: S:
Text: And so we have that policy.

Speaker: S:
Text: Now, the first school district in the state of Florida to do that was Polk County.

Speaker: S:
Text: That was in the early ‘90s, somewhere back then.

Speaker: S:
Text: And they were challenged, they were sued because a lot of the parents did not want the children to wear uniforms.

Speaker: S:
Text: And so they got together and they sued the school board.

Speaker: S:
Text: Well, the judge upheld for the school board, because they said that the school board have the right to determine what they think is best for their school districts.

Speaker: S:
Text: So, I knew that case.

Speaker: S:
Text: So, people were threatening me too, saying they were going to sue.

Speaker: S:
Text: But I knew that if they did, that it would be upheld, ‘cause it had already happened.

Speaker: S:
Text: And so that was one of the things that three of us thought would be best.

Speaker: S:
Text: And so we doing that and I’m happy about that.

Speaker: S:
Text: Those are three.

Speaker: S:
Text: Oh!

Speaker: S:
Text: And one other thing I’m really proud of is the fact that I was elected by my peers to become the president of the Florida School Board Association.

Speaker: S:
Text: I was presiding over all of the sixty-seven counties in the state of Florida.

Speaker: A:
Text: Oh, gosh.

Speaker: S:
Text: So I did that.

Speaker: S:
Text: That’s a year.

Speaker: S:
Text: You do that for a year.

Speaker: S:
Text: I had been a delegate to the national — actually, if I had not left, I was being primed for the National School Boards Association.

Speaker: S:
Text: I would have surely been that president, you know, but I left the board.

Speaker: S:
Text: Because there had been some turbulent times in the district and so I just was tired.

Speaker: S:
Text: And I wanted somebody else to come on and try to take over where I left off.

Speaker: S:
Text: However, I was asked to come back, so I tried it and I made it.

Speaker: S:
Text: And so here I am right now.

Speaker: A:
Text: Okay.

Speaker: A:
Text: When segregation was switching to integration everywhere around the country, how did you witness that?

Speaker: A:
Text: And how did it change?

Speaker: A:
Text: Did it change anything in everyday life?

Speaker: A:
Text: Or did it remain pretty much the same?

Speaker: S:
Text: The only thing that changed was that when I graduated, I graduated in a still-segregated school.

Speaker: S:
Text: I was never in an integrated school system until I went to college.

Speaker: S:
Text: But as far as high school and from my elementary on up, it was always segregated.

Speaker: S:
Text: So, I never experienced the changeover.

Speaker: S:
Text: And when my kids went to school, they went to school in an integrated system.

Speaker: S:
Text: So, they never experienced the segregated.

Speaker: S:
Text: So it’s kinda like I was kind of not, you know.

Speaker: S:
Text: But I understand the plight, though, of that, because that was turbulent times also.

Speaker: S:
Text: Because, just like all White people are not alike, all Black people are not either.

Speaker: S:
Text: And some of the White people didn’t mind their children, you know, integrating the school system, some of them did.

Speaker: S:
Text: And then some of the Blacks didn’t want to do it either because they had their own school, they loved their school, they didn’t have a problem or anything like that.

Speaker: S:
Text: But as it stood, the law was that the schools need to be integrated.

Speaker: S:
Text: And I think that was a good thing.

Speaker: S:
Text: And the reason I think it was because we all living on this earth.

Speaker: S:
Text: Why can't we -- why does it have to be separated?

Speaker: S:
Text: I don't think it was ever meant to be to start with.

Speaker: S:
Text: But all that came from slavery, plantationism, and all that kind of thing.

Speaker: S:
Text: So, back then, when our grandparents and great grandparents and all those — they had no choice whether they were slaves or not.

Speaker: S:
Text: And the one that tried to leave were probably shot and killed and pushed over boats in the water.

Speaker: S:
Text: You know, there are so many different things that happened which was not a good thing.

Speaker: S:
Text: But that's history.

Speaker: S:
Text: History, you can't change.

Speaker: S:
Text: Some people have avoided it.

Speaker: S:
Text: You might be able to omit it, but you cannot change it.

Speaker: S:
Text: It's there.

Speaker: S:
Text: It's etched in stone.

Speaker: S:
Text: So you can't change that.

Speaker: S:
Text: So there's been an omission, like even in some of the history books.

Speaker: S:
Text: I think it would help Black students a lot if they knew their real history and where they came from and how they got there.

Speaker: S:
Text: Because the history books really don't go through the detail of what really happened in the slavery days and the segregation and all that.

Speaker: S:
Text: Black people really had did a lot to contribute to history.

Speaker: S:
Text: But you'd have a hard time trying to find that in the history books.

Speaker: S:
Text: It should be there.

Speaker: S:
Text: So what parents need to be about the business of, even to this day, is trying to bring your kids up --

Speaker: S:
Text: Teach 'em at home.

Speaker: S:
Text: They don't have to wait till they get to school to find out there's nothing in there about them.

Speaker: S:
Text: Teach 'em at home.

Speaker: S:
Text: And if you don't know it, make yourself available.

Speaker: S:
Text: You can go to the libraries and find all that out.

Speaker: S:
Text: There's really no excuse now for kids coming to school not knowing anything about their history and not being prepared.

Speaker: S:
Text: It all goes back down to being prepared to come to school.

Speaker: S:
Text: Some of our kids, and this is not a Black issue alone, this is low socieeconomics.

Speaker: S:
Text: Poverty plays a key role in what is happening to students of low socioeconomic groups.

Speaker: S:
Text: Because all Black kids are not poor and all White kids are not rich.

Speaker: S:
Text: It is a conglomerate of children.

Speaker: S:
Text: And there a lot of these kids who come to school so unready to learn and it’s not their fault.

Speaker: S:
Text: Some of them are so drugged out when they get to school because of their parents, they couldn’t learn nothing if their life depended on it.

Speaker: S:
Text: But if some students can even learn their name in the run of a school term, that’s a lot.

Speaker: S:
Text: Because a lot of times you ask the kids, say, “What is your mother’s name?”

Speaker: S:
Text: “Momma.”

Speaker: S:
Text: That’s all they know.

Speaker: S:
Text: That’s not their fault.

Speaker: S:
Text: It’s their surroundings.

Speaker: S:
Text: And so a lot of them are being raised by their grandparents, who are lucky to be able to put food on the table for these kids, who give them shelter, and try to put clothes on their back, because it’s coming from their little Social Security checks.

Speaker: S:
Text: So everybody in this world, in this nation, in this county, is not doing well.

Speaker: S:
Text: We are not as bad off as a lot of people, but we are not that well off either.

Speaker: S:
Text: We’ve come a long way, but we still have a long way to go.

Speaker: S:
Text: But I’m considering where I’ve come from, and where I’ve been, and where I am now.

Speaker: S:
Text: I don’t worry about so much about what — even though I’m affected by everything that happened in the past, I don’t let that guide my life or the future.

Speaker: S:
Text: Because I can’t help what was, but I can help what is and what will be.

Speaker: S:
Text: So, that’s where I am right now.

Speaker: A:
Text: You mentioned grandparents.

Speaker: A:
Text: Can you tell me a little bit about your grandparents?

Speaker: S:
Text: My grandparents died, you know, early on.

Speaker: S:
Text: Yeah.

Speaker: A:
Text: So you never had the chance to meet them?

Speaker: S:
Text: I had a chance to meet them, but not to live around them so much.

Speaker: S:
Text: Yeah.

Speaker: S:
Text: But I had one that probably lived longer than any other of them, my grandmother in Quincy.

Speaker: S:
Text: She worked in the tobacco fields, and she was a very proud woman.

Speaker: S:
Text: She had very little education but she was able to get along with young people, old, anybody.

Speaker: S:
Text: They loved her.

Speaker: S:
Text: They called her “Momma Sis.”

Speaker: S:
Text: And she just believed in — when people come, they could be passing by, "Hey, Momma Sis!”

Speaker: S:
Text: “Hey, come on in and have something to eat.”

Speaker: S:
Text: She want to feed everybody.

Speaker: S:
Text: But, and she was really -- I learned a lot from her, too.

Speaker: S:
Text: How to be gracious and how to have pride in what you had, and she liked to dress and wear her hats to church and all this kind of stuff.

Speaker: S:
Text: She was a very proud woman.

Speaker: S:
Text: But she died.

Speaker: S:
Text: She had a heart attack.

Speaker: S:
Text: She went to one of her friend’s funeral and she had a heart attack the very day, right after she came back from the funeral and died right there.

Speaker: A:
Text: Oh gosh.

Speaker: S:
Text: Uh-huh.

Speaker: S:
Text: But, you know.

Speaker: S:
Text: And then my one grandfather lived in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, for a while.

Speaker: S:
Text: I wasn’t raised up around him but I knew him.

Speaker: S:
Text: And the other died, you know, before.

Speaker: S:
Text: My mother’s mother died when she was thirty with a heart attack, so I didn’t know her either.

Speaker: A:
Text: Do you know about what jobs they did?

Speaker: S:
Text: No, I don’ t, except my —

Speaker: A:
Text: The plantation?

Speaker: S:
Text: My grandma.

Speaker: S:
Text: Yeah, yeah.

Speaker: S:
Text: That’s all.

Speaker: S:
Text: I don’t know really what they did.

Speaker: A:
Text: I have a question about —

Speaker: S:
Text: Uh-huh.

Speaker: A:
Text: The election —

Speaker: S:
Text: Uh-huh.

Speaker: A:
Text: That just happened, with Obama.

Speaker: A:
Text: When he was running for president, were you supportive and do you feel like he’s — how do you feel about his current policy?

Speaker: S:
Text: I feel so proud that he was elected president, I don’t know what to do.

Speaker: S:
Text: I think he is a brilliant man, I think he is one among a lot of brilliant Black men.

Speaker: S:
Text: But I think for his position, that he is well-qualified for the job.

Speaker: S:
Text: And I think he inherited a lot of problems that could not be solved in the four years that he was elected to office.

Speaker: S:
Text: The president before him did the best he could, I believe, but it didn’t help.

Speaker: S:
Text: It didn’t help the problem that president Obama inherited.

Speaker: S:
Text: Politics are strange.

Speaker: S:
Text: Because he’s being blamed now for stuff that he had nothing to do with.

Speaker: S:
Text: And he’s got a Congress who is not willing to help him to get things done that needs to be done.

Speaker: S:
Text: And he is a guy that wants to be inclusive and expects things to just go smoothly for the sake of the country.

Speaker: S:
Text: Not for his sake, but for the sake of this country.

Speaker: S:
Text: But you have got some people who are so against him to start with, would rather see the country come to its knees than to stand up and help this man fight to get everything back on track.

Speaker: S:
Text: So that’s the way I see that.

Speaker: S:
Text: But I’m supportive of him.

Speaker: S:
Text: I was so happy to see him, being the first Black — even though he’s got mixed parentage and all of that, it’s okay.

Speaker: S:
Text: That’s fine.

Speaker: S:
Text: He’s got the “one-drop syndrome,” which qualifies him as being Black, so far as the history book says.

Speaker: S:
Text: So that’s how that goes.

Speaker: S:
Text: But I am proud of him.

Speaker: S:
Text: And hopefully he will overcome this, but it’s hard because he’s not used to having people, you know, in a position like the Congress is.

Speaker: S:
Text: And they’re all against him and they’re expecting him to do miracles that nobody did.

Speaker: S:
Text: They expect him to walk on water without insulting the environmentalists.

Speaker: S:
Text: And, you know, so he’s got a long row to hoe, but I think he’ll probably pull it off.

Speaker: S:
Text: But, I’m proud of him.

Speaker: A:
Text: Coming back to your position.

Speaker: A:
Text: Are you planning to run again?

Speaker: S:
Text: Uh-huh.

Speaker: A:
Text: Are you going to keep trying to —

Speaker: S:
Text: Yeah, I’m going to run again.

Speaker: S:
Text: This four year term will be up this November.

Speaker: S:
Text: However, I have to qualify.

Speaker: S:
Text: The qualifying date is June of 2012 and the primary is August 8th, I believe it is, this year.

Speaker: S:
Text: So I am going to run.

Speaker: S:
Text: I have not launched a full-fledged campaign yet because I’m trying to collect signatures.

Speaker: S:
Text: And to keep from having to pay that money, because it’s a lot.

Speaker: S:
Text: And so I’ll be doing that, but I am gonna run.

Speaker: A:
Text: Is there anything I didn’t cover that you would like to add?

Speaker: S:
Text: Let me see.

Speaker: A:
Text: Okay.

Speaker: S:
Text: What can I think of?

Speaker: S:
Text: I’m trying to remember.

Speaker: S:
Text: I said chess.

Speaker: S:
Text: I said Healthy Kids.

Speaker: S:
Text: I said about the Teachers’ Orientation.

Speaker: S:
Text: I said about the Florida School Boards Association president.

Speaker: S:
Text: I don’t know.

Speaker: S:
Text: I know I have seen a lot of changes, though.

Speaker: S:
Text: Because, some people think that just being on the school board is an easy job, but it is not.

Speaker: S:
Text: It’s not easy for the staff, it is not easy for the board, it’s not easy for the superintendent or his assistants.

Speaker: S:
Text: Because everybody is focused on what they’re doing and we are — and I am bragging about this.

Speaker: S:
Text: We have been as far as I know, for the longest time, been, I know ever since I’ve been on the board, we have been way up there in being, if not the best, next to the best.

Speaker: S:
Text: I think we are the best school district in the state of Florida.

Speaker: S:
Text: We are way ahead.

Speaker: S:
Text: We've always been forward thinkers.

Speaker: S:
Text: We've always managed to, some kind of way, not have to cut programs from our students.

Speaker: S:
Text: Programs and not have to lay people off like a lot of the other districts did.

Speaker: S:
Text: We've always tried to do our very best to stay.

Speaker: S:
Text: And we have things thrown at us every year because every time the legislature meets, you have new legislators.

Speaker: S:
Text: They come with their ideas.

Speaker: S:
Text: You have the one that's been on, you know, and they have their ideas too.

Speaker: S:
Text: But it seems like to me it's getting more and more, some kind of --

Speaker: S:
Text: I don't want to call it animosity, but it's more of a challenge for school boards now to even stay afloat.

Speaker: S:
Text: It appears to me like public schools are not in some people's estimation as important as it used to be.

Speaker: S:
Text: Even though the public schools have to try to educate every child that walks through our doors.

Speaker: S:
Text: It seems like there are those who want to believe that we have charter schools, which are better than the public schools.

Speaker: S:
Text: We have private schools, which they think are better.

Speaker: S:
Text: They think the parochial --

Speaker: S:
Text: But the thing is with that is we have to try to educate everybody.

Speaker: S:
Text: They don't.

Speaker: S:
Text: They can be selective.

Speaker: S:
Text: We can't.

Speaker: S:
Text: If we could be selective, who's not gonna go and try to get the best of the -- the cream of the crop.

Speaker: S:
Text: We would too, probably, but that's not us.

Speaker: S:
Text: We're the public schools.

Speaker: S:
Text: And a lot of the legislators, a lot of the presidents, a lot of the Congressmen, they went to public school.

Speaker: S:
Text: So what is it about public schools suddenly that is they're saying is not up to par and all that kind of thing?

Speaker: S:
Text: And so I don't agree with that, but I do think there is a way for us to work together.

Speaker: S:
Text: And that way is not for the school board to be belligerent with the legislature but to just line out our strategies and what we think ought to be helpful from them.

Speaker: S:
Text: But when you have people who jump up and down shouting that the legislator are telling them what they're doing, this and that, the other.

Speaker: S:
Text: Probably, they're gonna go the other way, 'cause I don't like it when people shout at me and tell me that I don't know what I'm doing, you know, and stuff like that.

Speaker: S:
Text: You need to know what you're talking about — you know what I mean?

Speaker: S:
Text: And so, hopefully that will get better and we'll be able to work together.

Speaker: S:
Text: Because I have seen when public schools — the education in public schools was on the front burner.

Speaker: S:
Text: But it's not even on the stove anymore.

Speaker: S:
Text: And it's getting to be — the universities, they're being targeted now, too.

Speaker: S:
Text: So I don't think it's a good thing.

Speaker: S:
Text: I think that we need to still have our children coming up, and the students at the universities, coming up so that they can contribute to society also.

Speaker: S:
Text: But what I would like to see is them stop putting all this stuff on us that these kids are not gonna use.

Speaker: S:
Text: Make it relevant!

Speaker: S:
Text: Education needs to be relevant.

Speaker: S:
Text: Why would I make somebody that is not even going to school — why would I want them to have geometry or whatever else?

Speaker: S:
Text: I see them having math, arithmetic, the basic — you know, stuff like that.

Speaker: S:
Text: But all this stuff that they're not gonna need to have in their fields?

Speaker: S:
Text: Let it be geared toward what they need and not just have something just to throw it up there and say they're gonna use it.

Speaker: S:
Text: Because nine times out of ten, what it causes kids to do, is when they start overburdening them with all that stuff, they drop out.

Speaker: S:
Text: And then they wonder why the dropout rate is so high.

Speaker: S:
Text: It's high because you're not gearing it toward what they need.

Speaker: S:
Text: We need vocation 'cause a lot of kids are not going to go to college.

Speaker: S:
Text: They don't wanna go, anyway, and they're not going.

Speaker: S:
Text: So, that promotes drugism because it’s lucrative.

Speaker: S:
Text: And if these kids don't -- if they get out there on the streets and they see where they can make a lot of money, they're gonna do it.

Speaker: S:
Text: And a lot of the parents are not gonna ask them when they bring it in, "Where is it coming from?”

Speaker: S:
Text: Because they need another meal on the table.

Speaker: S:
Text: So all those things we need to work together in doing.

Speaker: S:
Text: And stop blaming the schools for these children not learning.

Speaker: S:
Text: Blame these parents.

Speaker: S:
Text: It’s up to these parents to get these kids ready to go to school.

Speaker: S:
Text: They need to be ready when they come to us.

Speaker: S:
Text: Because when they're not, the teachers have to focus on those few who are disturbed mentally, by no fault of their own.

Speaker: S:
Text: But then the others who are ready get kinda, you know, they kinda like caught in the middle here.

Speaker: S:
Text: So we’re not perfect, but we're doing a lot for these children and I’m tired of people blaming us and they need to be putting the blame — they got mad at Bill Cosby because he was saying this blame needs to go on these parents.

Speaker: S:
Text: I’m with him one hundred percent.

Speaker: S:
Text: Because I think that’s what needs to be done.

Speaker: S:
Text: Now we’ve got one of our assistant superintendents here that writes articles, he writes fantastic articles.

Speaker: S:
Text: And he’s telling these people what they need to do.

Speaker: S:
Text: As a matter of fact, we are using his conference room right now.

Speaker: S:
Text: His name is Phil Wright.

Speaker: S:
Text: And he is very good at writing these articles, telling these people what they need to do.

Speaker: S:
Text: Stop blaming everybody.

Speaker: S:
Text: These are your kids!

Speaker: S:
Text: Stop being a sperm receptacle, and stop being a sperm donor.

Speaker: S:
Text: And if you are, take care of your children.

Speaker: S:
Text: You know what I mean?

Speaker: S:
Text: So much for that!

Speaker: S:
Text: Kelly, it was nice to meet you.

Speaker: A:
Text: Thank you so much for your time.

Speaker: S:
Text: Okay.

Speaker: S:
Text: And if you think of something else you need me for, call me, we’ll talk.

Speaker: A:
Text: Okay, thank you so much.

Speaker: S:
Text: You’re welcome.
